title: Indexes and query execution
problem: A query that should touch twenty rows reads the whole table, or the app fires one query per row, and nobody can tell which from the code alone.
summary: The planner turns SQL into a tree of scans and joins using statistics; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated against actual rows. Covering indexes enable index-only scans, selectivity decides when an index helps, and N+1 lives outside the planner's reach.
catTip: Before I pounce I check the floor plan: shortest path to the bowl, not the longest. EXPLAIN is the floor plan the database drew; if its guess of where the mice are is wrong, so is the route.

recall.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a nested loop whose inner index scan has loops=50000, while the outer node estimated 20 rows and produced 50,000. What went wrong and what do you do first?
recall.a: The planner's row estimate was far too low, usually from stale statistics or correlated columns, so it chose a nested loop that ran 50,000 times. Run ANALYZE, consider extended statistics on the correlated columns, and recheck the plan before adding indexes.

guide.breaks: Without a planner working from accurate statistics the database full-scans tables or loops an index lookup millions of times, and without reading the plan you optimise blind.
guide.tradeoffs: Every index speeds some reads and slows every write, covering indexes widen the index, and statistics are a sample, so estimates can be wrong exactly on the skewed data that matters.
guide.explainSimply: You tell the database what you want and a planner works out the route, like a satnav choosing between the motorway and side streets. EXPLAIN shows the route and how long each leg really took. If the satnav's map is out of date it picks a bad route, and refreshing the map (statistics) often fixes more than building new roads (indexes).
guide.hint: Compare what the planner expected with what actually happened, and look at how many times the inner loop ran.

meow: Seq scan, index scan, index-only if the index has it all. Rows estimated versus rows actual, meow: that gap is the bug.

quiz.prompt: A query filters orders by status, a column with three values where the chosen value matches about 40% of rows. The team adds an index on status, but EXPLAIN still shows a Seq Scan. Why?
options: The index is corrupt and must be rebuilt
Low selectivity: fetching 40% of rows individually costs more than reading every page once, so the planner correctly prefers the scan
PostgreSQL never uses an index until ANALYZE has run
Bitmap scans are disabled by default
quiz.explanation: An index pays off when it skips most pages; at 40% selectivity scattered fetches cost more than one sequential pass. A bitmap scan is chosen for middling selectivity, but 40% is still too much.

quiz.prompt: Which change turns an Index Scan into an Index Only Scan for SELECT status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42?
options: Adding status and total to the index with INCLUDE, provided the visibility map marks the heap pages all-visible
quiz.explanation: An index-only scan needs every referenced column in the index and all-visible heap pages; INCLUDE supplies the columns without widening the search key. work_mem affects sorts and hash tables, not scans.

cards.q: A page renders 50 orders and then runs 50 more queries to fetch each order's customer. Name the problem and two fixes.
cards.a: The N+1 problem: 1 + 50 round trips. Fix it with a JOIN that returns orders with their customers, a single batch query using WHERE id IN (...), or the ORM's eager loading (includes or preload).

cards.q: When does a hash join beat a nested loop, and what does Batches above 1 in a Hash node tell you?
cards.a: A hash join wins for large inputs joined on equality when the build side fits in memory; a nested loop wins when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. Batches above 1 means the hash table exceeded work_mem and spilled to disk.
